title: Merge safety: limits, gating, and follow-ups (scratch)
content:
Context: quick scratchpad for ideas / checks to reduce 'merge -> incident' cycles. Mostly heuristics and TODOs for follow-ups. Not polished; notes to self.

Top-line problem statements:
- Tends: small PRs touching batching/cache invalidation + routing often cause intermittent latency spikes post-merge.
- Root symptoms: unbounded request fanout, missing apply-order in cache invalidation, or failing fast path on partial failures.

High-level goals:
- Make merges low-blast: automated safety gates + simple human checklist for risky areas.
- Make post-merge triage predictable: clear rollback knobs, scoped canaries, and quick telemetry queries.

Quick heuristics for labeling risk (to auto-enforce gates):
- Label "blast-radius: high" if change touches: routing, cache invalidation, KV cache schema, request shaping, or release toggles.
- Label "performance-sensitive" for code paths that run on token path (generation, attention cache, kernel selection).
- Label "requires-smoke" for changes touching rollout/upgrade code.

Pre-merge checklist (short):
- [ ] Is there a unit/ci test that exercises the change in a short-path? (if no, add smoke test)
- [ ] Does this change alter request routing or do any client-facing redirects? If yes: add rollout plan + canary config.
- [ ] Any new config defaults? If yes: ensure conservative defaults and opt-in via feature flag.
- [ ] Is there a visible metric to detect regressions? (p90 latency / errored-requests / kv-hit-rate). If none, add a temporary metric or log marker.
- [ ] Add a small 'shock absorber' mitigation: e.g., token-bucket on path, quick circuit-breaker with 1-minute rolling window.

Automated gating ideas (CI / bot):
- Static analyzer rule: if diff touches files under infra/routing or cache/, require two approvers.
- Bot checks: for diffs > 200 lines that modify runtime/ or serving/, require 3 reviewers OR must pass a perf-smoke job (CI uses pareto sample of infra).
- CI perf-smoke: spin up a tiny devpool run (1-2 GPUs) with representative model + short sequence. Fails if p95 latency increases > 20% vs baseline.
- Label-driven workflow: when PR has label "blast-radius: high", automatically create a rollback-runbook checklist and require an owner on the PR.

Operational mitigations (post-merge):
- Canary window: default 30m for non-critical changes, 2h for high-risk. Must have a canary route and automatic rollback threshold on error-rate or latency.
- Fallback variants: keep a previous model/handler binary as fallback in routing table for 6 hours post-merge, with auto-failover on threshold.
- Quick rollback command: ./infra rollback --deploy <canary-id> --reason quick-revert (bind to infra-runbooks and SRE playbooks).

Observability checklist (must be added before merge if absent):
- [ ] p50/p90/p95 latency metrics for the route(s) touched
- [ ] request count and error budget burn (5m/1h)
- [ ] cache-hit ratio and cache-evictions count (if cache code changed)
- [ ] tracing span naming to find slow step (kernel selection, kv-load, batching).

Specific refactor ideas to reduce future risk:
- Introduce small adapter layer for cache invalidation with versioned keys (cache/v2/{resource}/{version}) to avoid in-place key changes.
- Consolidate routing rules into a single canonical matcher file + unit-tests that assert precedence for N cases (remove duplicated ad-hoc matchers).
- Make token-bucket / rate-limiters composable and declarative (yaml) per-route so we can tweak without code deploy.
- Add 'canary-mode' flag in runtime so you can route X% of traffic to new binary without changing infra routing tables.

Experiments to run (quick, cheap):
1) Controlled merge with synthetic load: merge to canary, replay 5 minutes of recorded traffic, verify p95 and error spike < threshold.
2) Fault-injection in CI: simulate slow kv-load and assert graceful degradation path triggers (circuit open) rather than cascading timeouts.
3) Small-scale chaos: artificially drop 10% of responses from a dependency to ensure caller retries/backoff behave.

Unresolved questions / tradeoffs (notes):
- How conservative should defaults be? Too conservative slows feature velocity; too permissive increases incidents. Need baseline data on how many post-merge incidents are severity >= P2.
- Perf-smoke CI is noisy and slow; we may only run on label or large-diff. Cost vs safety tradeoff to document.
- Can we expose per-PR canary windows in Console? That would reduce manual ops but requires UI/DB work.

Actions / next steps (short):
- [ ] Draft a small RFC for label-driven gating and perf-smoke CI (owner: me) — include cost estimate.
- [ ] Add two new static analyzer rules: enforce reviewer counts for certain paths (owner: Evan).
- [ ] Prototype token-bucket declarative config for a single high-traffic route (owner: Noah).
- [ ] Run one synthetic canary for last week's large merge (owner: Rina) to gather baseline numbers.

Snippets (copy into PR descriptions / CHECKLIST):
- Required PR description blurb: "Blast radius assessment: [low|medium|high]. Canary plan (route, percent, duration): __. Metric to watch: __. Revert command: infra rollback ..."
- Quick query to find suspect merges (placeholder): "SELECT merge_commit, p95_latency_change FROM deploy_metrics WHERE changed_files LIKE '%/cache/%' ORDER BY p95_latency_change DESC LIMIT 20"

Notes to self (one-liners):
- Keep friction low: don't gate tiny doc fixes. Use path-based rules.
- Start with opt-in for perf-smoke (label) and move toward mandatory for high-touch paths.
- We can automate creating quick runbooks in PR comments for high-risk merges (template with runbook links).

End of scratchpad. Will iterate into an RFC once I run the first synthetic canary and have numbers.

---
